Phishing awareness
DALUMAT • GROUP 2 — STEM

Don’t get hooked.

PhishLens helps you recognize suspicious emails, texts, phone calls, and links before you click, reply, download, or share something private.

Learn the signs Check links Test yourself
01 • LEARN

Know what the hook looks like.

Phishing is a trick: someone pretends to be trustworthy so you will click, reply, download something, or reveal information. The goal is not to make every message look fake — it is to make a risky request feel normal.

Think before you click
THE BIG IDEA

Phishing works by creating trust, pressure, or curiosity.

A scam can copy a school, bank, game, social platform, delivery service, friend, or even a person you know. What matters is the request: are you being pushed to do something unusual, secret, or difficult to verify?

EMAILTEXT / SMSPHONE CALLFAKE WEBSITE
1Get your attention. “Urgent,” “final warning,” “you won,” or “someone logged in.”
2Push a decision. Click, reply, call a number, open a file, or sign in.
3Collect something. Passwords, one-time codes, personal details, money, or access.
02

Common types of phishing

Different channels use the same basic trick in different ways.

Email phishing

Fake emails imitate organizations or people you recognize and often include a suspicious link, attachment, or request.

“Your account will be suspended today. Verify now.”

Text / SMS scams

Short messages rely on urgency because people tend to read and react to texts quickly.

“Reply with the code we just sent you.”

Phone scams

A caller may sound confident or helpful while asking for passwords, codes, payments, or personal information.

“I’m from support. Read me the code on your screen.”

Fake websites

A page can copy the colors, logo, and layout of a real service while sending your information to someone else.

Look-alike domain + unfamiliar sign-in page
03

Red flags worth noticing

One clue does not automatically prove a scam. Several together should make you stop.

Urgency

“Act in 10 minutes,” “last chance,” or “your account closes today.”

Unexpected contact

You did not ask for help, a prize, a security check, or a password reset.

Suspicious links

The visible name looks familiar, but the actual domain is strange or misspelled.

Secrets requested

Passwords, PINs, one-time codes, recovery codes, or other authentication details.

Money pressure

Unexpected fees, gift cards, transfers, or payment details are requested immediately.

Attachments

Unexpected files can be used to deliver malware or fake login pages.

Odd wording

Awkward grammar, unusual greetings, or details that do not fit the supposed sender.

Impersonation

A familiar name or logo is not proof. Verify the actual account, address, or number.

LINKS & WEBSITES

Do not trust the text on a button.

A message can say “School Portal,” “Bank Login,” or “Security Check” while the destination is completely different. On a computer, hover over a link when possible; on a phone, be cautious about tapping and use the official app or type the known website yourself.

Account securityhttps://campus-verify.example/loginLooks official at a glance. Check the real domain before signing in.
04

Words and requests to look out for

These are not automatically scams — they are reasons to slow down and verify.

UrgentVerify nowAccount suspendedUnusual sign-inConfirm your identityOne-time codePasswordRecoveryPayment requiredPrize / rewardClick this linkDownload attachmentFinal warningClaim nowSecurity checkGift card
05

What to do when something feels off

You do not need to prove that a message is a scam before you pause.

01

Pause

Do not let a countdown or emotional message choose for you.

02

Inspect

Check the sender, address, phone number, wording, link, attachment, and request.

03

Verify independently

Open the official app or website yourself, or contact the organization using a trusted number.

04

Report and delete

Use your school or service’s reporting tools, then remove the suspicious message.

DO

Use a trusted route

A message says your school account needs attention. Open the school portal yourself instead of using its link.

  • Check the official app or website.
  • Ask a trusted adult, teacher, or support channel if you are unsure.
  • Report the suspicious message.
DON’T

Hand over a secret

Do not send a password, one-time code, recovery code, or payment information because a message or caller demands it.

  • Do not click first and investigate later.
  • Do not call the number supplied by a suspicious message.
  • Do not assume a logo makes the request real.
SCENARIO

Your friend’s account sends you a strange link.

Even if the name is familiar, the account could be compromised. Verify through another channel before opening it.

SCENARIO

A caller says they need your one-time code.

Stop. A one-time code is used to prove that you are you. Never read it to an unexpected caller.

SCENARIO

A message says you won something.

Unexpected prizes that ask for money or personal details are a strong warning sign.
